name: CEO
role: Sets strategic direction and chairs the Board.
publicPosition: Supports transformation if it improves business capability.
underlyingConcern: AeroTech becoming a build-to-print supplier that loses ground on new programmes.
blindSpot: Underestimates how long organisational change takes to pay back.
challengeQuestion: How does your recommendation improve our competitive capability?

questions.text: What concerns you most about this decision?
questions.response: That we make the right call for the business. The Board wants a recommendation it can stand behind.

questions.text: What business problem are we actually trying to solve?
questions.response: Everyone talks about software features. I'm buying capability: contract wins, engineering effectiveness, resilience. Standing still worries me more than a bumpy year.

questions.text: What are competitors doing that AeroTech isn't?
questions.response: Several of our tier-2 rivals are investing heavily in integrated digital engineering. They're pitching that capability to our customers.

questions.text: Has that gap already cost AeroTech any work?
questions.response: Yes, though I don't advertise it. We lost a 2025 work package partly because we couldn't supply model-based definition data.

questions.text: What would make the Board reject every proposal presented to it?
questions.response: A team that hasn't understood implementation risk. And in my experience people fixate on the technology and underestimate the organisational side, because it's harder to put a number on.

name: Finance Director
role: Owns the investment case, cash flow and programme budgets.
publicPosition: Supports transformation only if the implementation risks are understood.
underlyingConcern: A repeat of the ERP rollout, where hidden costs appeared after approval.
blindSpot: Treats organisational capability as a cost rather than an asset.
challengeQuestion: Convince me this is not simply an expensive technology upgrade.

questions.text: What budget is available for the new platform?
questions.response: There's money pencilled in, but the number matters less than what it buys. Bring me a case, not a price.

questions.text: Which costs are easiest to underestimate in a programme like this?
questions.response: Lost productivity, implementation support and process redesign. When we rolled out ERP in 2023, engineering output fell about 20% for six months and none of it was in the budget.

questions.text: What financial question has nobody asked yet?
questions.response: How much of the budget funds technology versus organisational change. The current draft puts about 85% into licences and hardware.

questions.text: Which assumptions in a business case like this would concern you most?
questions.response: Any claim that benefits arrive quickly without disrupting operations. I've never seen it happen.

questions.text: How will the Board evaluate an investment of this size?
questions.response: Anything over £5M gets enhanced scrutiny and competes with our other strategic investments. And cheapest isn't automatically best if it forces a second transition later.

name: Chief Design Engineer
role: Leads design engineering and simulation for all customer programmes.
publicPosition: Supports capability growth but fears the productivity loss.
underlyingConcern: Missing a major Airbus milestone in the middle of a migration.
blindSpot: Underestimates how much the team's expertise depends on a few individuals.
challengeQuestion: How will my team keep delivering live programmes while learning a new system?

questions.text: How do you feel about changing platforms?
questions.response: Cautiously open. Capability matters, but so does keeping programmes on track.

questions.text: Which design capabilities are non-negotiable, whatever platform we choose?
questions.response: Complex surfacing, large-assembly performance and composite design. Without those we can't do the work we're paid for.

questions.text: Which dependencies are people ignoring when they talk about switching?
questions.response: Simulation. Our stress and fatigue work relies on scripted links between V5 and Abaqus. Change the platform and those links break until we rebuild and re-validate them.

questions.text: What would make this programme fail on the engineering side?
questions.response: Running a migration while we deliver. The next Airbus work package lands right in the middle of any realistic transition, and output will drop.

questions.text: How long before engineers are faster than they are today?
questions.response: Vendors say weeks. My honest estimate is 12 to 18 months. New software doesn't make anyone faster on day one.

name: Manufacturing Director
role: Runs CNC production and CAM programming at both sites.
publicPosition: Will oppose any strategy that threatens delivery.
underlyingConcern: Undocumented shop-floor knowledge being lost in the migration.
blindSpot: Underestimates the long-term cost of the inefficiencies the shop floor has learned to work around.
challengeQuestion: What happens if implementation impacts production delivery?

questions.text: How would you measure success for this programme?
questions.response: Minimal production disruption, and fewer inefficiencies between engineering and the shop floor.

questions.text: What could stop production during a migration?
questions.response: Engineering can tolerate disruption; factories can't. Our Airbus and Rolls-Royce schedules don't pause for a software project.

questions.text: Which assumptions about manufacturing worry you?
questions.response: That every workflow can be recreated easily somewhere else. Much of our capability lives in processes, not software, and every migrated NC program must be proven on the machine again.

questions.text: Where is that process knowledge actually held?
questions.response: In people's heads and in unofficial macros. About 400 NC programs go through in-house post-processors that nobody has ever documented.

questions.text: Which platform characteristic matters most to manufacturing?
questions.response: Integration across the engineering and manufacturing lifecycle. Every manual hand-off costs us rework and scrap, and over-cautious governance slows down every attempt to fix them.

name: Quality Manager
role: Owns AS9100 certification, configuration control and customer audits.
publicPosition: Will oppose any strategy that creates compliance uncertainty.
underlyingConcern: Being blamed for an audit finding caused by someone else's project.
blindSpot: Treats every change as risk, and underestimates the risk of standing still.
challengeQuestion: What evidence supports your confidence in compliance continuity?

questions.text: How does quality fit into this decision?
questions.response: Every change has governance implications. My job is to make sure we stay certified.

questions.text: What hidden work do engineering teams usually overlook in changes like this?
questions.response: Procedures, training records, configuration controls, audit evidence. All of it needs rewriting, and it's never in the engineering plan.

questions.text: What would failure look like from a quality perspective?
questions.response: Losing confidence in configuration control. If a migrated model can't be traced to its released configuration, that's a major audit finding.

questions.text: What would auditors expect to see during the transition?
questions.response: That nothing about our obligations changed: AS9100 still applies on day one of any migration. And that we can still open archived V5 data for the 20-year life of the parts.

name: HR Manager
role: Responsible for recruitment, retention and skills development.
publicPosition: Concerned with capability development and recruitment.
underlyingConcern: Losing experienced engineers before their knowledge is passed on.
blindSpot: Assumes a training plan will be enough to carry people through change.
challengeQuestion: Who will train 220 engineers, and what happens to morale while they learn?

questions.text: Will staff need training on a new system?
questions.response: Of course. We'd put a plan together, as we would for any new system.

questions.text: Which skills gaps worry you over the next five years?
questions.response: Experience. Eight of our 25 most experienced CATIA engineers could retire within five years, and a lot of what they know isn't written down.

questions.text: How do our current tools affect recruitment?
questions.response: More than people admit. Graduates arrive trained on newer tools, and two candidates turned us down last year citing our ageing software.

questions.text: Could training existing staff close that gap on its own?
questions.response: I doubt it. Training budgets don't attract people who expect modern tools. And retraining 220 users is 6 to 10 days each plus super-user support, during peak delivery.

name: IT Manager
role: Responsible for infrastructure, security and software lifecycle.
publicPosition: Increasingly concerned about lifecycle and supportability.
underlyingConcern: Being left to support an ageing estate with shrinking vendor help.
blindSpot: Sees the decision as an infrastructure project and underestimates the people side.
challengeQuestion: How will you keep defence-related data compliant on the new platform?

questions.text: Is the IT infrastructure ready for a new platform?
questions.response: Broadly. Any new platform will need some infrastructure work, but nothing we can't plan for.

questions.text: What support risks does IT face if nothing changes?
questions.response: V5 is moving to sustaining support. Fewer fixes, and no guarantee it'll run on future Windows releases.

questions.text: How should lifecycle management influence this decision?
questions.response: A current platform would make patching and licence administration far simpler. Today I keep unsupported workstation builds alive just to run old V5 add-ins.

questions.text: What would limit a cloud-hosted option?
questions.response: Our BAE Systems work. Defence-related data has to stay in UK-controlled environments, which rules out some hosting models.

name: Airbus Representative
role: Airbus supplier development lead for AeroTech's programmes.
publicPosition: Focused on long-term digital capability in the supply chain.
underlyingConcern: A key supplier slipping on delivery while it transforms.
blindSpot: Underestimates what digital transformation costs a supplier of AeroTech's size.
challengeQuestion: How well will this recommendation serve AeroTech in ten years rather than one?

questions.text: How is the relationship with AeroTech going?
questions.response: Positive. AeroTech is a reliable supplier and we value that.

questions.text: Which capability trends matter most to Airbus over the next decade?
questions.response: Collaboration across increasingly digital supply chains. Frankly, a supplier that fails to evolve worries us more than one that spends money changing.

questions.text: Would AeroTech's software choice influence supplier selection?
questions.response: Not directly. We don't mandate a CAD tool. We judge the capability the tools enable.

questions.text: What concerns customers when a supplier goes through a transformation?
questions.response: Delivery. During a transformation, delivery performance matters more to us than technology ambition.

questions.text: Which assumption should AeroTech challenge in its own thinking?
questions.response: That our expectations will stay where they are. Supplier digital requirements will look very different within the decade.

name: Senior CAD Engineer
role: Twenty years on CATIA; the go-to expert for tooling and part-family design.
underlyingConcern: Quietly favours retaining CATIA-derived workflows, and their own standing as the expert.
blindSpot: Underestimates how hard it is becoming to recruit engineers who want to work in V5.
challengeQuestion: Have you asked the people who actually use the software every day?

questions.text: Do you enjoy working in CATIA V5?
questions.response: It does everything we need. Our processes are proven, and the team knows them inside out.

questions.text: What would make a migration difficult in practice?
questions.response: Today's workflows work well, but plenty of them are personal: templates, macros and part-family tables people built themselves. They live on individual machines.

questions.text: Which workflows are most valuable to the business, even if nobody manages them?
questions.response: The post-processors. About 400 NC programs run through in-house macros nobody ever documented. I'd hate to see them lost.

questions.text: How would your colleagues really respond to a migration?
questions.response: Between us? Most of the senior team expect it to be scaled back or reversed. They'd go along with it, but slowly.

name: Graduate Engineer
role: Second-year graduate in the design team.
publicPosition: Today's workflows may not suit future engineers.
underlyingConcern: Building a career on tools the rest of the industry is leaving behind.
blindSpot: Underestimates certification, process stability and the cost of disruption.
challengeQuestion: Will your recommendation help AeroTech keep its next generation of engineers?

questions.text: What do you think of the current tools?
questions.response: They're fine. A bit dated compared with what I used at university.

questions.text: What attracts new engineers to an employer like AeroTech?
questions.response: Modern, connected tools signal a company that's going somewhere. Today's workflows won't suit the engineers you'll need to hire.

questions.text: Why have people from your cohort turned down offers here?
questions.response: Two friends of mine said no last year. Both mentioned the software, which they saw as a dead end for their CVs.

questions.text: What would a new platform not fix?
questions.response: Honestly? I'd assumed newer software would just make us all faster. I haven't thought much about what it wouldn't fix.
